description: Can we imagine a world without coral reefs? The projections are grim. At current warming trajectories, over 90% will be dead by 2050. The good news is that restoration works. The challenge is whether we can make it work fast enough. A new generation of technology is making it possible to grow coral colonies in months rather than decades, breed for heat resistance, and deploy AI to monitor reef health at a global scale. The reefs our children inherit will depend on the work we do right now, while there is still magic left to save. Gator Halpern is the co-founder and President of Coral Vita, a land-based coral farm that grows reef-building corals up to 50 times faster than conventional methods using micro-fragmentation and assisted evolution techniques. Coral Vita operates farms in the Bahamas and is scaling production with KAUST University in Saudi Arabia toward 400,000 coral colonies per year. He holds a degree from Yale University and has worked with reef restoration programs across
title: How to train your coral: lessons from an AI-driven aquaculture farm | Gator Halpern | TEDxBoston

description: Fitted with one of the first satellite collars, a wild wolf named Ploy trekked 100,000 kilometers before being legally shot just outside a national park boundary. Her journey proved that national parks are essential, precious, but nowhere near big enough. When a bold proposal emerged to protect an area three times the size of California across national and international borders, it seemed far-fetched. How could you coordinate and cooperate at that scale? The Yellowstone to Yukon (Y2Y) project is proving what's possible, growing its protected areas by more than 80% over 30 years through the work of more than 800 partners. And that's just the beginning.  Jodi Hilty is President and Chief Scientist of the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative, which works to connect and protect wildlife habitat across a 3,200-kilometer corridor spanning Wyoming, Montana, Idaho, British Columbia, Alberta, and the Yukon. She holds a PhD in ecology and has spent more than 25 years working on large la
title: Wildlife need room to roam. It's time to rethink conservation at scale. | Jodi Hilty | TEDxBoston

author: TEDx Talks
description: The math doesn't math: globally, eight billion people depend on just nine crops for two-thirds of their diet. Historically, humans ate 50,000 different plants. Inside an Arctic mountain near the North Pole, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds the genetic backup for a food system that has become dangerously narrow and now even more fragile in the face of climate instability. But the seeds are only half the story. This is a place where North Korean assets rest alongside those from South Korea, where Ukraine and Russia share shelf space. Peruvian farmers entrusted Svalbard with their sacred potatoes, plants treated as kin. It is a precious shared endeavor that supersedes global conflict and human lifespan. What can the project teach us about inspiring trust in science and the power of international cooperation at a moment when both are under attack? Adriana Craciun is a Professor of English at Boston University and one of the few outside researchers granted access to the Global Seed Vau
title: A growing library of civilization carved deep into an arctic mountain | Adriana Craciun | TEDxBoston

author: TEDx Talks
description: For hundreds of years, human development has rushed water off the land by draining wetlands, levying rivers, paving floodplains, and drying soil with industrial agriculture. Along with rampant deforestation, our choices have degraded as much as 75% of Earth's land, and even disrupted the reliability of the planet's own natural cooling and rainfall systems. When tropical rainforests 'exhale' water vapor, those particles seed rain that falls on crops thousands of miles away. The living systems that regulate our water, our weather, and our food supply are deeply connected, and we have been quietly dismantling them. Author Erica Gies calls this "The Great Drying". The good news is we can reestablish water systems and rehydrate the land, starting with even small interventions. Slowing water, allowing it to sink in, and restoring the living systems that work within it can help mitigate the increasingly severe effects of floods, droughts, and wildfires. Hear inspiring stories of deep repair
title: We broke the rain meddling with the planet's cooling system. What now? | Erica Gies | TEDxBoston

A tree that saved 150 lives. A tree that sheltered robbers. A tree worth ₹100 crore. A tree that inspired strangers across the world to come together and protect it.
Over 40,000 kilometres and 150 remarkable trees later, Uday Krishna discovered something unexpected: the story of trees is ultimately the story of us. Through The Big Tree Quest, he uncovers living witnesses to history that have survived empires, shaped communities, and quietly protected humanity for centuries. At TEDxHyderabad's Fire Up, this talk sparks a different kind of urgency not to admire trees from a distance, but to notice what we stand to lose before it's gone. Uday Krishna is an environmental storyteller, conservation advocate, and founder of the Vata Foundation, dedicated to protecting India’s natural heritage through community-driven action. Deeply connected to the wilderness, he advances conservation through wildlife photography, jungle rejuvenation, and immersive storytelling.

description:
O que faz alguém dedicar a própria vida à proteção de uma causa maior do que si mesmo? Nesta palestra, Angelo Rabelo compartilha sua trajetória de anos em defesa do Pantanal, enfrentando desafios, riscos e adversidades em nome da conservação ambiental. Em uma reflexão sobre propósito, resiliência e compromisso, ele mostra como a decisão de continuar, mesmo diante das dificuldades, pode gerar impactos duradouros para pessoas, comunidades e para um dos biomas mais importantes do planeta. Angelo Rabelo dedicou a vida à proteção do Pantanal. Coronel da reserva da Polícia Militar de Mato Grosso do Sul, atuou na linha de frente do combate aos crimes ambientais na região, onde chegou a ser ferido por um tiro em confronto durante operações de proteção da fauna e da natureza e quase perder a vida. 

Depois de consolidar importantes avanços na proteção do bioma, decidiu ampliar essa missão e fundou o Instituto Homem Pantaneiro, organização dedicada à conservação do bioma e à valorização da cult
title: Uma vida pelo Pantanal: propósito, resiliência e decisão de continuar | Angelo Rabelo | TEDxCarandá

description: In her talk, Mbali Dhlamini traces the arc of artistic obsession: the pursuit of a single plant species - Indigofera. This plant is not merely a material resource for her practice but the object of an enduring fixation that both drives and sustains her creative work; work that uses art to preserve indigenous knowledge and systems, and expand conversations. Her account situates obsession within an artistic research framework as a deliberate, focused enquiry that blurs the line between discovery and compulsion. Dhlamini performs visual, tactile and discursive investigations into current indigenous cultural practices. Working to maintain a state of unlearning and relearning, Dhlamini's process recognises language as a medium of understanding and as a repository of knowledge. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx
